lessons.title: Young King Henry and the Rise of Wolsey

before.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Describe Two Features question on Henry’s accession or Wolsey’s rise, give two distinct features and one supporting detail for each — do not waste time explaining causes, that is the 8-mark question. For a 16-mark Make and Defend a Judgement on why Wolsey rose so quickly, weigh his ability against Henry’s temperament, then add a third factor of your own (such as his clerical wealth or lack of noble rivals) to push above the top stimulus and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
before.content_html:
When Henry VIII inherited the throne on 22 April 1509, he was just seventeen, athletic, musical, fluent in Latin and trained in theology. England greeted him as a Renaissance Prince — a stark contrast to his cautious, miserly father. Within weeks the new king had married his brother’s widow, Catherine of Aragon, and signalled an immediate break from Henry VII’s style. Two of his father’s most hated tax collectors, Empson and Dudley, were arrested and later executed. The message was clear: a different reign had begun.

Key Fact

Henry VIII became king on 22 April 1509, aged seventeen. He married Catherine of Aragon on 11 June 1509 and was crowned alongside her on 24 June.

England in 1509: Society and Government

Tudor England in 1509 was a population of roughly two and a half million, overwhelmingly rural, organised through a steep social hierarchy that ran from the king at the top, down through the nobility and gentry, to yeomen, husbandmen and the poor. Government rested on the king’s personal authority. The monarch ruled with the help of the Royal Council, called Parliament when he needed taxes or major laws, and relied on Justices of the Peace and bishops to enforce his will in the localities. The Church, headed in England by the Archbishop of Canterbury but in spiritual obedience to the Pope in Rome, owned around a quarter of the land and shaped daily life from baptism to burial.

Henry’s Character and Aims

Henry styled himself as the model Renaissance Prince: a warrior, a scholar and a patron of the arts. The Italian humanist Erasmus admired his Latin; the Venetian ambassador Sebastian Giustinian called him “the handsomest potentate I ever set eyes on”. But behind the dazzle lay a sharp set of aims. Henry wanted military glory in France, a male heir to secure the Tudor dynasty, and personal control of his kingdom without the day-to-day grind of administration. Where Henry VII had been content to manage paperwork, his son preferred hunting, jousting and music. He needed someone to do the work.

His view of sovereignty was uncompromising. Henry believed God had given him absolute authority over England. He expected obedience from nobles, bishops and Parliament alike. This conviction would later drive both the break with Rome and the harsh treatment of any minister who failed him.

Strengths: Henry inherited a stable throne, a full treasury (Henry VII left around £1.5 million), and no serious rival claimants. He was charismatic, well educated and physically imposing — useful theatre in an age when monarchy depended on personal display.

Weaknesses: He was inexperienced, easily flattered, and impatient with detail. He dreamed of recapturing the French crown his ancestors had lost, but the Treasury could not sustain a long war. His desire for glory needed a manager who could find the money, the ships and the alliances. That manager would be Thomas Wolsey.

Wolsey’s Rise from Ipswich

Thomas Wolsey was born around 1473 in Ipswich, the son of a butcher and innkeeper. This was an extraordinary starting point for a man who would dominate Henry’s government. Educated at Magdalen College, Oxford, he took priest’s orders and entered royal service as a chaplain to Henry VII. His real opportunity came in 1513. Henry VIII wanted to invade France, and Wolsey, as Royal Almoner, organised the supply of an army of 30,000 men — ships, food, ordnance, transport — with brisk efficiency. The campaign captured Thérouanne and Tournai and produced the Battle of the Spurs, a small but flashy English victory. Henry got his glory; Wolsey got his attention.

Promotion came in a torrent. Bishop of Lincoln in 1514, Archbishop of York that same year, Cardinal in 1515, and Lord Chancellor in 1515 — the senior office of state. In 1518 the Pope appointed him papal legate for life, giving him authority over the English Church above even the Archbishop of Canterbury. By the early 1520s he was effectively running England’s government, foreign policy and Church.

Key Fact

By 1518 Wolsey held four major offices: Archbishop of York (1514), Cardinal (1515), Lord Chancellor (1515) and papal legate (1518). No commoner had ever combined this much Church and state power.

Why Did Wolsey Rise So Fast?

Several factors combined. First, sheer ability: Wolsey was intelligent, energetic and a tireless administrator who could draft a treaty in the morning and chair a court case in the afternoon. Second, he understood Henry. He flattered the king, kept him supplied with hunting parties and pageants, and quietly absorbed the workload Henry disliked. Third, his clerical career gave him an income independent of royal grants — the archbishopric of York, the bishoprics he held in plurality, and the wealth of his palaces at Hampton Court and York Place funded his court without bleeding the Crown. Fourth, he had no powerful family. As a butcher’s son he depended entirely on Henry’s favour, which made him easier to trust than the great noble houses with their rival claims.

His personality was a contradiction. Contemporaries describe Wolsey as proud, ostentatious, and quick to crush opponents — he insisted on processing through London with two crosses, four cushions, and trumpeters. Yet he was also a serious lawyer, a real reformer in justice and finance, and a diplomat capable of holding his own with Francis I and Charles V. Geoffrey Cavendish, his gentleman usher and biographer, captured both sides: the man who lived “more like a prince than a priest” but who also served his king with relentless industry.

A common student error is to treat Wolsey as a puppet. The evidence shows otherwise. Wolsey shaped the foreign policy direction of the 1510s and 1520s, drove the Eltham Ordinances, and ran the law courts on his own initiative. Henry set the broad goals — war with France, glory abroad, a male heir — but Wolsey decided how. Historians like John Guy treat the relationship as a working partnership, with Wolsey enjoying real agency until policy began to fail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Henry VIII’s character and aims at his accession in 1509.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for a valid identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content (any two with valid detail):
• Renaissance Prince image — trained in Latin, theology and music; admired by Erasmus; styled himself as warrior-scholar.
• Desire for military glory — particularly recapturing English claims in France; led to the 1513 invasion.
• Need for a male heir — married Catherine of Aragon in June 1509 to secure the Tudor dynasty.
• Belief in personal sovereignty — saw himself as God’s anointed monarch, expecting obedience from nobles, Church and Parliament.
• Dislike of administrative detail — preferred hunting and pageantry, requiring a chief minister to handle the workload.

Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail; one may be more developed than the other.
Developing: Two features identified but detail thin or generic.
Emerging: Only one feature, or features with no supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Wolsey’s rise to power between 1509 and 1518.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, plus 1 for supporting detail. Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Organisation of the 1513 French campaign — supplied an army of around 30,000, leading to the capture of Thérouanne and Tournai.
• Rapid Church promotion — Bishop of Lincoln (1514), Archbishop of York (1514), Cardinal (1515), papal legate (1518).
• Appointment as Lord Chancellor in 1515 — the senior office of state, giving Wolsey control of justice.
• Independent clerical wealth — income from York and other sees funded his court at Hampton Court without draining the Crown.
• Personal closeness to Henry — absorbed routine business so the king could pursue hunting, jousting and music.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate dates or names.
Secure: Two features with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague or partially inaccurate.
Emerging: Only one feature, or unsupported.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Henry VIII relied on Thomas Wolsey to manage government in the 1510s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of the Spurs (1513)
• Henry’s personal style of government
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explanation of distinct, supported reasons. The two stimulus points must be developed and at least one independent reason added to reach the top band.

Indicative content:
• 1513 French campaign — Wolsey, as Royal Almoner, organised supply for an army of 30,000 men, including ships, food and ordnance. The capture of Thérouanne and Tournai and the Battle of the Spurs gave Henry the military glory he craved and proved Wolsey could deliver large-scale projects.
• Henry’s personal style — the king preferred hunting, jousting and pageantry to paperwork. A chief minister who could absorb the daily grind of council, courts and finance was indispensable.
• Wolsey’s administrative ability — he could draft treaties, chair the Court of Chancery and run foreign policy simultaneously, releasing Henry from detail.
• Wolsey’s lack of noble family — as a butcher’s son he had no rival power base, making him easier to trust than the Howards or Suffolks.
• Wolsey’s independent income — the archbishopric of York and the cardinalate funded his court without bleeding the Treasury.

Mastering: Three or more reasons, each clearly explained with specific evidence; sustained focus on ‘why’ rather than narrative; both stimulus points developed and own information integrated.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant detail; mostly explanatory; uses both stimulus points.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanations underdeveloped or descriptive in places.
Emerging: General narrative of events with little focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Henry VIII’s style of monarchy was different from his father’s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Empson and Dudley
• Henry’s Renaissance education
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Personal image and pageantry — Henry VIII used jousting, music and court spectacle to project a Renaissance Prince image, contrasting with Henry VII’s austere, paperwork-heavy style.
• Treatment of Empson and Dudley — Henry VII’s notorious tax collectors were arrested days after the new king’s accession and later executed, signalling a populist break from his father’s fiscal regime.
• Renaissance education — Henry VIII was fluent in Latin, trained in theology and admired by Erasmus, encouraging humanist scholarship at court rather than mere account-keeping.
• Aggressive foreign policy — where Henry VII avoided war, the new king sought military glory in France and committed Crown finances to it.
• View of sovereignty — Henry VIII saw himself as God’s anointed and demanded a more visible, theatrical assertion of royal supremacy than his cautious father.

Mastering: Sustained explanation of three or more reasons, with precise detail and clear comparison to Henry VII; both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons explained with relevant evidence.
Developing: Reasons identified but with limited explanation or supporting detail.
Emerging: Mostly description of Henry VIII without comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey was able to combine such great Church and state power by 1518.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the office of Cardinal
• Wolsey’s relationship with Henry VIII
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained, supported explanation of three or more reasons.

Indicative content:
• Cardinal’s hat (1515) and papal legate (1518) — gave Wolsey ecclesiastical authority above even the Archbishop of Canterbury, allowing him to summon Church courts and appoint to benefices.
• Lord Chancellor (1515) — the senior secular office, putting him in charge of the Court of Chancery and royal justice.
• Henry’s confidence — the king trusted Wolsey because he delivered the 1513 French campaign and entertained him with pageantry, freeing the king from administration.
• Independent wealth — income from York, Lincoln and other sees funded Hampton Court and his diplomatic establishment without drawing on the Treasury.
• Lack of rival noble family — as a butcher’s son Wolsey had no dynasty of his own, so concentrating offices in one man did not create a rival power base.
• Pope’s willingness — Leo X granted the legateship for life in 1518, hoping to use Wolsey to keep England within the Habsburg-Valois balance.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence and clear weighting; both stimulus points developed; own information adds substance beyond the prompts.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation and supporting detail.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy; some narrative.
Emerging: Limited reasons; explanation thin or descriptive.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the named factor against alternatives and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Henry preferred hunting, jousting and music to paperwork; council records show Wolsey routinely chairing meetings the king did not attend.
• Henry needed a manager to deliver the 1513 French campaign; Wolsey’s organisation of supply for a 30,000-man army made him indispensable.
• Henry’s Renaissance Prince image required pageantry rather than administration, leaving a vacuum Wolsey filled.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Wolsey’s personal ability — intelligent, energetic, a trained lawyer and theologian; he could not have risen without genuine talent.
• Independent clerical wealth — the archbishopric of York and bishoprics in plurality funded his establishment without depleting the Crown, making his power sustainable.
• Lack of a rival noble family — his butcher’s-son origins meant Henry could entrust him with great offices without creating a dynastic rival.
• Papal cooperation — Pope Leo X granted the legateship for life in 1518, allowing Wolsey’s domination of the English Church.

Overall judgement: Henry’s temperament created the opportunity, but Wolsey’s ability and clerical wealth allowed him to fill it; without all three the rise would not have happened. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Argument addresses the statement and at least one alternative; conclusion reached but weighting may be uneven.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; little or no argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Wolsey's Domestic Policy and the Justice System

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Why question on the Eltham Ordinances, do not just describe what they did — the question rewards why. Three explained reasons (efficiency, economy, factional control) beat one beautifully described one. Use period-specific vocabulary — ‘Privy Chamber’, ‘ordinances’, ‘commissioners’ — rather than vague paraphrase such as ‘Henry’s inner circle’ or ‘rules’. The SPaG mark on 16-mark questions is awarded for exactly this kind of vocabulary, so practise it on shorter questions too.
before.content_html:
As Lord Chancellor from 1515, Thomas Wolsey ran the daily business of England: he chaired the king’s council, presided over the senior law courts, raised taxation, regulated wages and prices, and tried to reform the royal household. His domestic record is the most contested part of his career. To his admirers he was an energetic reformer who opened justice to the poor and modernised royal finance; to his critics he was a self-serving bully who stretched the law and stored up enemies. Both pictures contain truth.

Justice: Chancery and Star Chamber

Wolsey poured most of his judicial energy into two prerogative courts. The Court of Chancery, which he chaired as Lord Chancellor, judged cases on principles of fairness, or equity. It was attractive to litigants who could not afford the slow, expensive common-law courts: a widow cheated of her dower, a tenant evicted by an over-mighty landlord, a small landowner crushed by a powerful neighbour. Under Wolsey the volume of Chancery cases roughly doubled.

The Star Chamber, which met at Westminster in a room decorated with gold stars, was Wolsey’s instrument for disciplining the powerful. It dealt with cases the local common-law courts dared not touch — nobles enclosing common land, gentry intimidating juries, riots and corrupt officials. Wolsey personally heard around 120 cases a year, compared with about 12 a year under Henry VII. Famously, he made an example of the Earl of Northumberland in 1515 for retaining illegal armed followers, and humiliated Sir Amyas Paulet by forcing him to wait for hours at Wolsey’s chamber door.

Key Fact

Wolsey expanded the Court of Chancery, which judged cases on equity, and the Star Chamber, which disciplined powerful nobles. Both bypassed the slow common-law courts and made justice more available to ordinary people.

In the short term, yes. Cheap, fast equity drew thousands of cases and the Star Chamber genuinely curbed the worst noble abuses. In the longer term the system overheated — courts were swamped, common-law judges resented the encroachment, and Wolsey’s personal style invited accusations of bias. Critics argued that he favoured petitioners willing to pay clerks generously. After his fall, the volume of Star Chamber business shrank.

Enclosure: The 1517 Commission

Enclosure — the conversion of arable common land to sheep pasture — was a flashpoint of the period. Sir Thomas More attacked it bitterly in Utopia (1516): “Your sheep, that were wont to be so meek and tame and so small eaters, now become so great devourers and so wild that they eat up and swallow down the very men themselves.” In 1517 Wolsey launched a national commission to investigate enclosures since 1488. The commissioners gathered evidence in 28 counties and prosecuted 264 landowners in Chancery, ordering them to restore their land to tillage.

The result was symbolic rather than transformative. Many cases dragged on for years; some landowners simply paid fines and continued enclosing. Yet Wolsey signalled to the Crown’s subjects that the powerful would not be left unchecked, and to landowners that even great men were within the king’s reach. By 1523 he had to compromise — abandoning enforcement to win Parliament’s support for war taxation.

Finance: The Subsidy

Henry’s wars were ruinously expensive. To pay for them Wolsey overhauled royal taxation. The medieval ‘fifteenth and tenth’ raised a fixed sum regardless of changing wealth and bore most heavily on the poor. Wolsey replaced it with the subsidy, a tax assessed on each taxpayer’s actual income from land, goods or wages. Tax commissioners visited each parish to record wealth, and the rate could be varied to match need. In 1523 Wolsey demanded an unprecedented £800,000; Parliament resisted, and only around £200,000 was eventually raised over four years — still a huge sum for the period.

The subsidy was a genuine fiscal innovation that survived into the seventeenth century. But it had limits. Each new round needed Parliament’s consent, taxpayers learned to undervalue their property, and Wolsey’s 1523 demand exhausted political goodwill. The 1525 Amicable Grant — covered in the next lesson — was a forced response when Parliament refused another subsidy.

Key Fact

Wolsey’s subsidy taxed people on their actual wealth, replacing the flat-rate fifteenth and tenth. Between 1513 and 1529 it raised around £325,000 — far more than any earlier system — but Parliament always controlled how much was granted.

The Eltham Ordinances, 1526

In January 1526 Wolsey issued the Eltham Ordinances, a set of household regulations drafted at Eltham Palace. They reorganised the king’s domestic establishment, cut waste, set wages and food allowances, and reduced the number of gentlemen of the Privy Chamber from twelve to six. Officially the aim was efficiency and economy in royal expenditure. Unofficially, contemporaries noticed something more pointed: the men ejected from the Privy Chamber happened to include several who were challenging Wolsey’s influence over Henry, including William Compton, Henry Norris and the rising Boleyn faction.

Once the immediate political moment passed, many of the dismissed gentlemen drifted back to court. Historians like John Guy treat the Ordinances as a mixture of genuine administrative reform and factional self-defence — a textbook example of why Wolsey accumulated enemies even as he served the king well.

Each reform was real but limited. The Star Chamber expansion overloaded itself. The 1517 enclosure commission produced prosecutions but few lasting changes on the ground. The subsidy raised more money but ran into political resistance. The Eltham Ordinances were quietly diluted within months. Wolsey was a serious reformer who repeatedly failed to make his reforms permanent — partly because Henry’s priorities (war, prestige) kept overriding administrative consistency.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey reformed royal taxation through the subsidy.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the cost of war with France
• the limits of the ‘fifteenth and tenth’
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Cost of war — the 1513 French campaign and the 1520s wars far exceeded what the medieval fifteenth and tenth could raise; the subsidy was needed to fund Henry’s ambitions.
• Limits of the fifteenth and tenth — this older tax raised a fixed sum regardless of how wealth had shifted, leaving the rich under-taxed and the poor over-burdened.
• Equity — Wolsey wanted a tax assessed on individuals’ actual landed and movable wealth, surveyed by commissioners, so the burden matched ability to pay.
• Royal authority — a tax based on personal assessment increased the king’s knowledge of his subjects’ wealth and tightened central government’s grip.
• Wolsey’s reforming instinct — he was a trained administrator who saw the older tax system as outdated and inefficient.

• over-mighty subjects

practice_questions.marks:

Indicative content:

• Discipline of over-mighty nobles — Star Chamber could try powerful men whom local courts feared (e.g. Earl of Northumberland 1515), reasserting royal authority.
• Royal income and authority — expanded prerogative courts increased the Crown’s reach and provided fees that Wolsey could direct.
• Speed and accessibility — petitioners liked Chancery because cases moved faster and cheaper than common law.
• Wolsey’s personal stake — running these courts allowed him to project his own authority and keep the king’s justice visibly active.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Wolsey’s domestic policies created opposition by the late 1520s.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1517 enclosure commission
• the Eltham Ordinances
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Enclosure commission — landowners prosecuted in Chancery resented Wolsey’s interference and bought their way out, breeding cynicism rather than reform.
• Eltham Ordinances — the courtiers Wolsey ejected from the Privy Chamber (Compton, Norris and rising Boleyn allies) became long-term enemies once they returned.
• Subsidy assessments — commissioners’ valuations and Wolsey’s £800,000 demand of 1523 angered MPs and gentry alike, fuelling parliamentary resistance.
• Star Chamber prosecutions — high-profile humiliations of the Earl of Northumberland and Sir Amyas Paulet built a reservoir of noble grievance.
• Personal style — ostentation, two crosses, palaces grander than the king’s, and unilateral decision-making invited the charge of arrogance.
• Pluralism — holding multiple bishoprics simultaneously offended ecclesiastical reformers and Common-law lawyers wary of clerical encroachment.

Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.

‘Wolsey’s domestic policies were more successful than they were unsuccessful.’

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs successes and failures and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘more successful’:
• Star Chamber genuinely curbed noble abuses and made justice more accessible — cases rose tenfold to around 120 a year.
• Court of Chancery offered cheaper, faster equity remedies for ordinary petitioners; case volume roughly doubled.
• Subsidy taxed actual wealth and raised around £325,000 between 1513 and 1529 — the most successful Tudor tax innovation before the Civil War.
• Eltham Ordinances cut household waste and modernised the Privy Chamber.
• 1517 enclosure commission gave the Crown a moral authority over landowners that no previous government had attempted.

Arguments for ‘more unsuccessful’:
• Enclosure prosecutions produced fines but little lasting change on the ground.
• 1523 subsidy demand triggered fierce parliamentary resistance, raising only a quarter of what was asked, and led to the disastrous 1525 Amicable Grant.
• Eltham Ordinances were quietly reversed within months as ejected gentlemen returned.
• Star Chamber overloaded itself; common-law judges resented prerogative encroachment.
• Wolsey’s methods built up enemies (Northumberland, Paulet, Boleyns) who would help destroy him in 1529.

Overall judgement: Wolsey was a real reformer whose individual measures often worked in the short term; but most failed to become permanent because his political style created enemies faster than the reforms could win allies. lessons.title: The Amicable Grant and the Limits of Wolsey's Power

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Why on the failure of the Amicable Grant, three explained reasons (the size of the demand, lack of parliamentary consent, the East Anglian cloth recession) score better than one well-described one. For 16-mark judgement questions, treat 1525 as one factor in Wolsey’s decline and weigh it against the failed annulment in 1529 — do not narrate the events; argue why each mattered. Use period-specific vocabulary throughout: ‘non-parliamentary’, ‘subsidy’, ‘commissioners’, not ‘tax inspectors’.
before.content_html:
In the spring of 1525 Wolsey demanded a non-parliamentary tax so unpopular that it triggered open revolt across East Anglia, forced Henry VIII to back down within weeks, and revealed for the first time that the cardinal’s authority had limits. The Amicable Grant is a small episode with a large lesson: even at his height, Wolsey could not override the political nation when he asked too much.

Why Did Wolsey Need More Money?

In February 1525 the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V won a sensational victory over Francis I of France at the battle of Pavia. The French king was captured, his army shattered, and France lay vulnerable. Henry VIII saw the moment for a long-cherished dream: to invade France, claim the French crown, and join Charles V in dismembering the kingdom. He demanded an army within months.

The problem was money. Parliament had only just granted the 1523 subsidy, which was still being collected and had raised far less than hoped. Calling Parliament again so soon was politically impossible — MPs had openly resisted Wolsey’s demands two years before. Wolsey therefore proposed a non-parliamentary tax, which he carefully labelled the ‘Amicable Grant’ to suggest a friendly, voluntary contribution to the king’s war.

Key Fact

The Amicable Grant was demanded in March 1525 to fund Henry’s planned invasion of France after Charles V’s victory at Pavia. Parliament had refused another subsidy, so Wolsey tried to bypass it.

What Was Demanded?

The terms were severe. Clergy were asked to pay one-third of their incomes; laymen one-sixth of theirs. There was no consultation, no parliamentary consent, and no upper or lower limit on individual assessments — commissioners simply fixed sums and demanded payment. Worse, this came on top of the still-unfinished 1523 subsidy. To many of Wolsey’s subjects it looked like the same tax, demanded twice, by a minister who had decided he no longer needed Parliament’s permission.

Resistance began almost immediately. In Kent, when the commissioners arrived, taxpayers cited Magna Carta and refused to pay without parliamentary consent. In London the city merchants protested. The greatest trouble came in East Anglia, the centre of England’s cloth industry, where economic recession and high unemployment meant taxpayers had nothing to give.

The East Anglian Revolt

By early May 1525, around 4,000 men had assembled at Lavenham in Suffolk in open revolt. They were led by John Greene and John Coxford, but the wider mood was one of communal resistance. The Dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk were sent north to confront the rebels; recognising that this was not a feudal rebellion against the king but a tax strike, the dukes opened negotiations rather than engaging in battle. The rebels insisted they were loyal to Henry — they would pay any tax legally granted by Parliament, but not this. The dukes had little choice but to agree.

Within days of the rising, Henry VIII abruptly cancelled the Amicable Grant. He claimed in public that he had never authorised it — a transparent rewriting of the record — and that Wolsey alone bore responsibility. The contrast was stark: Henry kept the credit for clemency; Wolsey absorbed the blame.

It was not. The leadership came from yeomen, clothiers and small employers, supported by clergy who themselves resented the one-third demand. The rebels invoked Magna Carta, refused to march on London, dispersed when the Grant was cancelled, and were not seriously punished. This was a tax revolt of the political nation — the people whose consent Tudor government depended on — not a populist uprising. That is precisely why it was so dangerous to Wolsey.

Consequences for Wolsey’s Power

The collapse of the Amicable Grant had three serious consequences. First, the planned invasion of France was abandoned. Henry never crossed the Channel in 1525, and within months Charles V signed the Treaty of Madrid with Francis I, leaving England with no return on Wolsey’s preparations. The diplomatic humiliation was profound.

Second, Wolsey’s reputation was permanently dented. The episode showed the political nation that the cardinal could be defied; it showed Henry that Wolsey could trigger crises; and it gave his enemies, especially the Duke of Norfolk and the rising Boleyn faction, a stick with which to beat him. The historian C.S.L. Davies argued that 1525 marks the beginning of Wolsey’s political vulnerability, even though his fall lay four years away.

Third, the constitutional principle that taxation needed parliamentary consent was vividly reasserted. Subsequent Tudor governments — including Henry VIII himself in the Reformation Parliament of 1529–36 — would work through Parliament far more carefully. The Amicable Grant was, paradoxically, a moment when the political nation taught the Crown a lesson about its own limits.

Key Fact

The collapse of the Amicable Grant cancelled the 1525 invasion of France, damaged Wolsey’s political standing, and reasserted the principle that taxation required parliamentary consent. Henry blamed Wolsey alone — a warning sign of how the king would one day let him fall.

G.W. Bernard’s 1986 study War, Taxation and Rebellion in Early Tudor England argued that the Amicable Grant was a watershed: it showed Tudor government could not collect direct taxation without parliamentary consent, and forced Wolsey to retreat from the most ambitious tax demand of the early sixteenth century. C.S.L. Davies and John Guy treat the episode as the moment Henry first publicly distanced himself from his minister — rehearsing, on a small scale, the move he would make against Wolsey in 1529 and against Cromwell in 1540.

lessons.title: Wolsey's Foreign Policy: Peacemaker or Warmonger?

before.exam_tip_html: For 16-mark Make and Defend a Judgement on whether Wolsey was a peacemaker or warmonger, do not split the answer 50/50 and shrug. Pick a position, support it with two clear examples and a third independent factor, then weigh the strongest counter-argument before reaching your overall judgement. Use period-specific vocabulary throughout: ‘papal legate’, ‘Habsburg-Valois rivalry’, ‘non-aggression pact’, not ‘peace agreement’. The SPaG mark rewards exactly this terminology.
before.content_html:
Foreign policy was the area in which Wolsey most directly served Henry VIII’s personal ambitions — and the area in which his successes were greatest, his failures most painful, and the historiographical debate most lively. Was Wolsey a Renaissance peacemaker who used diplomacy to make a second-rate kingdom matter in Europe? Or a warmonger who chased his master’s glory until reality bit back? The truth is more interesting than either label.

Wolsey’s Aims Abroad

Wolsey served two sets of aims at once. Henry’s aims were straightforward and old-fashioned: military glory, the recovery of English claims in France, and a male heir whose rule could not be threatened. Wolsey’s own aims were more sophisticated — to position England as the balance between the two great European powers, France under Francis I and the Habsburg empire under Charles V, so that England could broker peace and shape European affairs without bearing the full cost of war.

There is also a third strand sometimes mentioned by historians: Wolsey’s personal hope, encouraged by Pope Leo X’s grant of legateship for life, that he might one day become Pope himself. Twice in the 1520s — in 1521 and 1523 — he was a candidate at papal conclaves, and twice the Habsburg interest blocked him. Whether or not this drove his diplomacy, the prospect coloured his relationships with Charles V and the papacy.

Key Fact

Wolsey’s foreign policy aimed to satisfy Henry’s desire for glory, to make England the broker between France and the Habsburgs, and (probably) to advance Wolsey’s own ambition for the papal throne.

The Treaty of London, 1518

Wolsey’s diplomatic masterpiece was the Treaty of London of October 1518. Pope Leo X had proposed a five-year truce among Christian princes to prepare a crusade against the Ottoman Turks, who had captured Belgrade and threatened central Europe. Wolsey turned the papal idea into something larger and more permanent. He summoned ambassadors of more than twenty European powers — France, the Holy Roman Empire, Spain, the papacy, the major Italian states, the German princes, the Swiss cantons — to London. They signed a non-aggression pact: any signatory who attacked another would face combined retaliation by the rest.

The treaty made Henry the public guarantor of European peace, and Wolsey personally the broker. The pope’s plan had been overshadowed; Wolsey kept the credit. For a kingdom of two and a half million people sitting on the edge of Europe, it was a remarkable diplomatic coup. Judged by the realistic aim — making Henry a major European broker despite England’s modest power — the treaty was a triumph.

The Field of the Cloth of Gold, 1520

Two years later, Wolsey staged perhaps the most spectacular diplomatic theatre of the sixteenth century. Between 7 and 24 June 1520, in a valley near Calais, Henry VIII and Francis I met for two and a half weeks of jousting, wrestling, music, banquets and Mass under a tent of cloth-of-gold thread. Around 6,000 English and 6,000 French courtiers attended; a temporary palace was constructed for Henry; great fountains ran with wine. The cost to England alone was approximately £15,000 — about a fifth of annual royal revenue.

The Field of the Cloth of Gold was a magnificent display, but it was theatre, not policy. Almost as soon as Henry returned to England he met Charles V at Gravelines, and within two years he was at war with France. The summit cemented Wolsey’s reputation for spectacle but did nothing to alter the underlying Habsburg-Valois rivalry.

This is a trap students fall into. Judged by what England could realistically achieve, the Treaty of London was a triumph — it made Henry a European arbiter for the first time since the Hundred Years War. The peace lasted four years before being undermined by the death of Maximilian (1519), Charles V’s election as Emperor, and the renewal of Habsburg-Valois conflict in Italy. None of these factors was within Wolsey’s control. The collapse was not a Wolsey failure; it was the structural condition of European politics.

Increasing Difficulties in the 1520s

The 1520s steadily eroded the 1518 settlement. The election of Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519 created a single ruler over Spain, the Netherlands, Austria and parts of Italy — a Habsburg colossus that France could not tolerate. War broke out between Charles and Francis in 1521, and England was dragged in on the imperial side. Wolsey’s 1522–23 invasion of France under the Duke of Suffolk reached as far as Montdidier — only fifty miles from Paris — before supply collapsed and the army turned home.

By 1525 the alliance with Charles V had also collapsed. After the Battle of Pavia, Charles refused to share the spoils with Henry, leading directly to the failed Amicable Grant. Wolsey then reversed England’s alliance, signing the Treaty of the More with France (1525) and the League of Cognac (1526) to restrain Habsburg power. The diplomatic somersault was forced rather than chosen, and made England look unreliable. The 1527 Sack of Rome by Charles V’s troops left Pope Clement VII in imperial custody — a disaster for Wolsey, since the pope’s independence was essential for the planned annulment of Henry’s marriage to Catherine of Aragon. By the late 1520s Wolsey’s European balancing act had become a series of expensive course corrections, none of them yielding the male heir Henry actually wanted.

Key Fact

Wolsey’s 1520s foreign policy ran into trouble because of Charles V’s 1519 imperial election, the renewal of Habsburg-Valois war from 1521, and the 1527 Sack of Rome — all events outside his control but for which Henry held him responsible.

Older accounts from the early twentieth century treated Wolsey as either a self-aggrandising warmonger or a Renaissance internationalist; modern revisionist scholarship sees him as a pragmatist trying to balance Henry’s warlike instincts against England’s real resources. Peter Gwyn’s 1990 study argues that Wolsey was a serious diplomat working with very limited material; John Guy treats foreign policy as the area in which Wolsey was most clearly his own master, even when forced to deliver Henry’s wars.

before.content_html:
By 1527 Henry VIII had decided that his marriage to Catherine of Aragon must end. Within two years that decision — known to contemporaries as the King’s ‘Great Matter’ — had wrecked Wolsey’s career, brought England into open conflict with the papacy, and set the country on the road to the Reformation. The story is not just about Henry’s desire for a male heir; it is about how the failure of one annulment broke the most powerful minister in early Tudor England.

Catherine of Aragon and the Succession Problem

Catherine of Aragon had been Henry’s wife since 1509. She had borne him six children, but only one — Princess Mary, born 1516 — survived infancy. By the late 1520s Catherine was in her early forties and had not been pregnant since 1518. To Henry, the message was clear: there would be no male heir from this marriage. England had only ever been ruled by one queen regnant, the disastrous Empress Matilda in the 1140s, whose reign produced civil war. Henry believed a female successor would invite another Wars of the Roses.

There was also a religious anxiety. Catherine had first been married to Henry’s elder brother Arthur, who died in 1502. Pope Julius II had granted a special dispensation to allow her marriage to Henry. By 1527 Henry had convinced himself that this dispensation was invalid, citing the Old Testament book of Leviticus: ‘If a man shall take his brother’s wife, it is an unclean thing … they shall be childless.’ The lack of a son was, he argued, divine judgement on a marriage God had never sanctioned.

Key Fact

Henry sought an annulment, not a divorce. He argued that his marriage to Catherine of Aragon — his late brother’s widow — had been forbidden by Leviticus, and that Pope Julius II had no power to dispense with God’s law. The lack of a male heir was his evidence.

Why an ‘Annulment’ and Not a ‘Divorce’?

Period vocabulary matters here. Henry did not ask for a divorce in the modern sense; he asked for an annulment — a declaration that the marriage had never been valid in the first place. Only the Pope could grant such a ruling. From 1527 Henry pressed Wolsey to obtain one. Wolsey, as Cardinal and papal legate, was the obvious instrument: he had handled English business with Rome for fifteen years and had the connections to make a discreet ruling possible.

Pope Clement VII and the Sack of Rome

Wolsey’s timing could hardly have been worse. In May 1527, just weeks before Henry began his campaign, the unpaid army of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V mutinied and sacked Rome itself. Pope Clement VII fled to the Castel Sant’Angelo and emerged a virtual prisoner of the emperor. Crucially, Charles V was Catherine of Aragon’s nephew. Granting Henry his annulment would mean publicly humiliating Charles’s aunt, just as Charles’s troops controlled the papacy. Clement VII had every reason to delay and no political cover to decide.

Wolsey nevertheless persuaded Clement to send a second legate, Cardinal Campeggio, to England in 1528 to hear the case alongside him. Campeggio’s instructions from Rome, however, were to delay rather than decide. He travelled slowly, arrived in October, and spent months trying to persuade Catherine to take the veil and retire to a convent. Catherine refused absolutely. She insisted, in public and in private, that her marriage to Arthur had never been consummated and that her marriage to Henry was therefore valid in every way.

The annulment was the trigger, but the eventual break with Rome rested on overlapping pressures: the succession crisis, Henry’s claim to royal supremacy, fiscal opportunity from church wealth, and a real evangelical current at court led by Cranmer and later Cromwell. The historian Diarmaid MacCulloch emphasises that Cromwell held genuine reformist convictions; G.W. Bernard sees Henry himself driving the religious change. Either way, ‘the divorce caused the Reformation’ is too simple.

The Blackfriars Court, 1529

In May 1529 the legatine court finally opened at Blackfriars in London. The proceedings were extraordinary: a Queen of England summoned to defend her marriage. Catherine appeared on 21 June, knelt at Henry’s feet, and made a speech that became famous. She declared that she had been a true and obedient wife, that she had been a virgin when Henry first took her to bed, and that she could expect no impartial judgement in his realm. She then walked out of the court and refused to return. The case continued without her.

Through July, Wolsey and Campeggio worked through the legal arguments. On 23 July, just as Wolsey expected to deliver judgement, Campeggio adjourned the court for the Roman summer recess. Days later, news arrived that Clement VII had revoked the case to Rome. The Blackfriars court would never reconvene. England’s most powerful minister had been outmanoeuvred in front of his king.

Key Fact

The Blackfriars legatine court of May–July 1529 collapsed when Cardinal Campeggio adjourned proceedings for the Roman summer and Clement VII recalled the case to Rome. Wolsey had failed to deliver the only thing Henry now wanted.

The Boleyn Faction and Wolsey’s Enemies

By the time Blackfriars collapsed, Wolsey’s position at court had already been undermined. Anne Boleyn had been Henry’s preferred future queen since 1526 or 1527. Her father, Thomas Boleyn, and uncle, the Duke of Norfolk, led a faction at court that resented Wolsey’s monopoly of patronage. They also blamed him personally for failing to deliver the annulment quickly. Anne herself believed — with some reason — that Wolsey had only paid lip-service to her cause and was secretly working for a French marriage instead.

The Fall, October 1529

Within weeks of the Blackfriars failure, Wolsey was finished. In October 1529 he was charged under the medieval statute of praemunire — technically, exercising foreign (papal) jurisdiction without royal consent. It was a transparent political device, but a legally watertight one: as papal legate, Wolsey had spent fifteen years doing exactly what the statute forbade. He surrendered the Great Seal, lost the chancellorship to Sir Thomas More, and forfeited Hampton Court and York Place to the king. He retreated to his archbishopric of York. In November 1530, summoned south on charges of treason, he died at Leicester Abbey on the journey, sparing Henry a public execution.

John Guy treats the failure of the annulment as the immediate, sufficient cause: Henry needed a son and Wolsey could not deliver. Eric Ives stresses Anne Boleyn’s direct role in poisoning Henry’s mind against the cardinal. C.S.L. Davies sees Wolsey’s fall as the predictable end of a system in which all power flowed through one minister: when that minister failed once on a major issue, the whole edifice was vulnerable. The Amicable Grant of 1525 was the first warning shot; the failed annulment of 1529 was the killing blow.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks: Reward sustained argument that weighs the failure of the annulment against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Arguments for ‘most important’: • The annulment was the only matter Henry cared about by 1529; failure on it stripped Wolsey of his usefulness. • Campeggio’s adjournment of Blackfriars and Clement’s revocation of the case happened weeks before the praemunire charge. • The legal mechanism that removed Wolsey (praemunire, his papal legateship) only had teeth because the papal route had failed. • The annulment crisis brought the Boleyn faction directly into Henry’s confidence and cut Wolsey off. • Henry’s personal anger over Blackfriars is well documented in contemporary letters. Arguments for alternative explanations: • Influence of the Boleyns — Anne, Thomas Boleyn and the Duke of Norfolk had worked against Wolsey since 1526–27, undermining him long before Blackfriars. • Long-standing unpopularity — the Amicable Grant of 1525, ostentation (Hampton Court), pluralism, and monopoly of patronage had built broad opposition. • Henry’s personal style — he had publicly disowned Wolsey over the Amicable Grant in 1525, signalling that the cardinal was always expendable. • Charles V’s control of the papacy — structural; no English minister could have delivered an annulment under those conditions, so Wolsey’s fall was inevitable. • Foreign policy failure — the post-Pavia diplomatic isolation in 1525–27 weakened Wolsey before the annulment ever began. Overall judgement: the failed annulment was the immediate trigger, but it was decisive only because the Boleyn faction, the king’s readiness to disown ministers, and Wolsey’s broader unpopularity made him impossible to defend. Top-band answers will weigh these factors explicitly and reach a justified conclusion. Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout. Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached. Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing. Emerging: Largely descriptive.

before.content_html:
In 1529, when Wolsey fell, no one expected Thomas Cromwell to rule England. He had no royal blood, no Cambridge degree, no church preferment, and a master who had just been disgraced. Five years later he was Henry VIII’s most trusted minister, the engineer of the break with Rome, and arguably the most powerful commoner in English history. The story of how he got there is a story about loyalty, parliamentary skill, and a willingness to give the king what every other adviser said could not be done.

Putney Origins and Early Career

Cromwell was born around 1485 in Putney, then a village outside London. His father Walter was variously a blacksmith, a brewer, a fuller and a frequent defendant in the local manor courts — not poor, but not respectable either. By his early twenties Thomas had left England for the continent. He spent time as a soldier in Italy, a clerk in a Florentine bank, a cloth merchant in the Low Countries, and learned Latin, Italian, French and the workings of European commerce in the process. These were not the qualifications of a Tudor minister; they were the qualifications of a man who would think differently from one.

Back in London by around 1514, Cromwell built a legal practice and entered Wolsey’s service in the early 1520s. He worked on the cardinal’s pet project: dissolving small monasteries to fund Wolsey’s new colleges at Oxford and Ipswich. The work taught him three things he would later use on a national scale — how to value monastic property, how to draft Acts of Parliament, and how to manage royal commissioners on the ground. By 1529 he was Wolsey’s most trusted secular agent.

Key Fact

Cromwell rose from a Putney commoner background through trade, soldiering and law on the continent, then through service to Wolsey. He had no university degree and no church living — unusual for a Tudor minister.

Surviving Wolsey’s Fall

When Wolsey fell in October 1529, Cromwell looked finished. Most of the cardinal’s servants scattered or hid. Cromwell did the opposite. He stayed at his master’s side, organised the legal defence, and worked openly to limit the damage. He also — according to the contemporary chronicler George Cavendish — wept publicly for Wolsey, then took horse for Westminster to fight for a place in the new order.

The gamble paid off. Henry was impressed by the loyalty — loyalty to a fallen patron was, paradoxically, the best evidence that Cromwell would later be loyal to him. Within weeks Cromwell had secured election to the new Reformation Parliament, sitting first as MP for Taunton in November 1529. The seat was a back-bench borough; the platform it provided was not.

From the Commons to the Council

Through 1530 and 1531 Cromwell built his reputation in the Commons. He drafted bills, marshalled votes, and demonstrated a mastery of parliamentary statute that no one in royal service could match. By the end of 1530 he was a sworn member of the Royal Council, attending its meetings and trusted with sensitive royal business. By April 1532 he was Master of the King’s Jewels, controlling part of the royal finances. By 1533 he was Chancellor of the Exchequer.

The promotions tracked his usefulness. Cromwell offered Henry something Wolsey, More and the bishops could not: a route to the annulment that did not run through Rome. The argument was statutory. If Parliament could declare that England was a self-sufficient empire whose king answered to no foreign prince, then no English court — not even Cardinal Campeggio’s — needed papal permission to rule on the king’s marriage. By 1532 this was an idea Henry was prepared to act on. Cromwell drafted the legislation that turned it into law.

Henry VIII was not led by his ministers, but he was not their puppet-master either. Diarmaid MacCulloch’s 2018 biography argues Cromwell shaped the legal architecture of the break with Rome and quietly promoted his own evangelical religious convictions, including the English Bible. Geoffrey Elton went further in 1953, calling Cromwell the architect of a ‘Tudor revolution in government’. Revisionists like John Guy and David Starkey have softened that claim — the changes were piecemeal, not a planned revolution — but few historians now treat Cromwell as merely the king’s clerk.

Handling the Annulment, 1532–33

Cromwell’s breakthrough year was 1532. The Submission of the Clergy, drafted under his direction, forced the English Church to accept that no canon law could be made without royal assent. In August 1532 Archbishop Warham died; Henry, on Cromwell’s advice, appointed Thomas Cranmer — an evangelical sympathetic to the king’s case — in his place. Anne Boleyn was already pregnant by January 1533. Cranmer pronounced Henry’s marriage to Catherine void on 23 May 1533, his marriage to Anne valid five days later, and Anne was crowned on 1 June. The Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533), drafted by Cromwell, made it illegal to appeal any English legal case — including the annulment — to Rome.

Chief Minister, 1534

In April 1534 Cromwell was appointed Principal Secretary, an old office he transformed into the central coordinating role of Tudor government. By 1535 he was also Vicegerent in Spirituals — the king’s deputy in church affairs, with authority over every bishop in England. From these two posts he ran domestic government, foreign correspondence, royal finances and church reform simultaneously. No previous minister had concentrated so many functions in one office. By the time of the Act of Supremacy (November 1534), Cromwell was the king’s chief minister in everything but title.

Key Fact

By 1535 Cromwell was Principal Secretary, Master of the Rolls and Vicegerent in Spirituals. He coordinated government, finance, foreign correspondence and church reform from a single desk — a concentration of power without precedent.

Geoffrey Elton emphasised Cromwell’s mastery of statute and his transformation of Parliament into the engine of state. Diarmaid MacCulloch stresses Cromwell’s evangelical conviction — not merely a careerist but a believer who used office to advance a religious cause. John Guy and David Starkey argue the rise was contingent and circumstantial: Cromwell happened to offer Henry the right solution at the right moment, and the constitutional changes were driven by short-term need rather than long-term plan. The truth probably combines all three: a gifted lawyer with a religious agenda, in the right place at the right time.

glossary_terms.definition: The Parliament summoned by Henry VIII in November 1529, which sat in seven sessions until 1536 and passed the legislation of the break with Rome.
An Act of Parliament — a law passed by both Houses and given royal assent. Cromwell would make statute the central engine of Tudor government.
A 1532 declaration extracted from the English clergy that they would make no new church laws without royal assent — the first major statutory step against papal authority.
Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533, leading evangelical, drafter of the Book of Common Prayer; he annulled Henry’s first marriage in May 1533.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the annulment against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘most important’:
• The annulment was Henry’s overriding goal in 1532–33; Cromwell’s parliamentary route succeeded where Wolsey’s legatine route had failed.
• Cranmer’s elevation to Canterbury in 1533, secured on Cromwell’s advice, delivered the annulment in May 1533.
• The Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) was drafted by Cromwell specifically to make the annulment legally binding without papal consent.
• Henry’s gratitude rewarded Cromwell with rapid promotions: Master of the Jewels, Chancellor of the Exchequer, Principal Secretary.
• Without the annulment, Cromwell would never have moved beyond mid-rank office.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Mastery of parliamentary statute — Cromwell’s rise depended on technical skill no rival possessed; this was structural, not occasional.
• Loyalty to Wolsey in 1529 — the gamble that won Henry’s confidence preceded any service on the annulment.
• Membership of the Royal Council from 1530 — gave him the access required to do anything else.
• Boleyn alliance — Anne and Thomas Boleyn championed him; without the faction, the annulment alone would not have secured his promotion.
• Religious conviction — MacCulloch argues Cromwell’s evangelicalism gave him an independent agenda that fitted Henry’s emerging religious policy.
• Office innovation — the Vicegerent in Spirituals (1535) reflected a structural reorganisation, not just a reward for the annulment.

Overall judgement: the annulment was the decisive opportunity, but Cromwell’s rise rested on a unique combination of legal skill, political loyalty and faction alliance that turned that opportunity into permanent office. lessons.title: Opposition to the Reformation: More, Fisher and Barton

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Why on the importance of opposition to the Reformation, link the three figures rather than listing them: Barton showed Cromwell would treat prophecy as treason, Fisher showed even bishops were not protected, More showed legal silence would not save a refuser. before.content_html:
Once Parliament made denying the royal supremacy a capital offence, principled refusal became dangerous. In 1534 and 1535 three of England’s most prominent religious voices — Elizabeth Barton, John Fisher and Thomas More — tested whether the new church would tolerate dissent. None of them survived. Their executions sent a clear message about the limits of permissible disagreement, and shaped how the wider English Reformation would proceed under Cromwell and Cranmer.

The Nun of Kent: Visions and Treason

Elizabeth Barton was a young Benedictine nun who had begun receiving visions in 1525. Her prophecies attracted respectful attention from senior figures, including Archbishop Warham and even Wolsey, and she had spoken with Henry VIII himself. Her visions were initially uncontroversial. After 1532, however, she began to prophesy that if Henry married Anne Boleyn, he would die within a month and lose his soul. Word of these prophecies spread through London and into the houses of leading Catholics.

Cromwell’s response was decisive. In November 1533 Barton and her circle — including her confessor, Edward Bocking — were arrested and forced to confess publicly at Paul’s Cross that her visions had been fabricated. In early 1534 Parliament passed an Act of Attainder, condemning her without trial. On 20 April 1534 Barton was hanged at Tyburn alongside five male supporters — an unprecedented execution of a woman for political prophecy. The case demonstrated that Cromwell would treat religious resistance as treason, even when the resister was a popular visionary.

Key Fact

Elizabeth Barton, the Nun of Kent, prophesied that Henry would die if he married Anne Boleyn. Cromwell had her arrested in November 1533, condemned by Act of Attainder, and hanged at Tyburn in April 1534 — a warning to all religious opponents of the annulment.

John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester

Of all the English bishops, only one openly defied the supremacy: John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester since 1504. Fisher had been Catherine of Aragon’s confessor and her most articulate defender at Blackfriars. He had also publicly defended papal authority since the start of the annulment crisis. Fisher had been peripheral to the Barton case, though he had received some of her prophecies and not reported them. In 1534 he refused to swear the Oath of Succession because the preamble denied papal authority.

Fisher was sent to the Tower of London in April 1534. While he was imprisoned, Pope Paul III — in a gesture that infuriated Henry — created Fisher a cardinal in May 1535. The new title sealed Fisher’s fate. He was tried for treason in June 1535 under the new Treason Act, convicted, and beheaded on 22 June. He was 75 years old. Even by Tudor standards, the execution of a sitting bishop — and a newly created cardinal — was a political shock that resonated across Catholic Europe.

Sir Thomas More: Principled Silence

Sir Thomas More had been Lord Chancellor from October 1529, succeeding Wolsey. He was a humanist scholar of European reputation, friend of Erasmus, and author of Utopia (1516). He had also been a fierce persecutor of English heretics. More resigned the chancellorship in May 1532, the day after the Submission of the Clergy, recognising that the direction of royal religious policy was incompatible with his conscience.

When the Oath of Succession was administered in April 1534, More refused it. His objection was specific: he would not swear the preamble, which denied papal authority, even though he was prepared to accept Anne Boleyn’s daughter Elizabeth as heir. He took refuge in legal silence. He told his interrogators that the law could not compel a man to swear against his conscience, that his silence implied no opinion, and that qui tacet consentire videtur — he who is silent is taken to consent. The argument was legally sophisticated and morally formidable. It also failed.

More accepted the new succession. What he refused was the supremacy — the doctrine that the king of England, not the Pope, was head of the Church. The distinction matters. More was a humanist Catholic, not a defender of Catherine; his fight was over papal authority, not the marriage. The 1535 Treason Act, which made denying the supremacy a capital offence, was the law under which he was condemned, and it made his attempt at silence inadequate.

More’s Trial and Execution

More was sent to the Tower in April 1534 and held for fifteen months. His trial took place at Westminster Hall on 1 July 1535 under the 1535 Treason Act. The decisive evidence was the testimony of Sir Richard Rich, the Solicitor-General, who claimed More had spoken against the supremacy in private conversation in his cell. More denied the charge under oath; he and his contemporaries believed Rich had perjured himself. The jury convicted him in fifteen minutes. More was beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535. His last reported words were that he died ‘the king’s good servant, but God’s first’ — a formulation that would shape Catholic remembrance of the Reformation for centuries.

Key Fact

More resigned as Lord Chancellor in May 1532, refused the Oath of Succession in April 1534 because of its preamble denying papal authority, and was convicted of treason on 1 July 1535 on the disputed testimony of Sir Richard Rich. He was beheaded five days later.

Cranmer, Cromwell and the Wider Impact

While the executions stamped out high-profile opposition, Cromwell and Thomas Cranmer reshaped the parish church. Cranmer’s 1536 Ten Articles introduced a moderate Protestant influence on doctrine, including a reduced number of sacraments and an emphasis on scripture. Cromwell’s royal injunctions of 1536 and 1538 ordered every parish to acquire an English Bible, teach the Pater Noster, Creed and Ten Commandments in English, and keep parish registers of births, marriages and deaths — an administrative innovation that survived into the twentieth century.

The result was a Reformation that combined ruthless enforcement with steady administrative change. Public dissent was treated as treason; quiet pastoral practice was reshaped through commissioners and visitations. By the late 1530s the English Church was unmistakably under royal control, with the parish life of ordinary people changing more slowly than the constitutional headlines suggested.

G.W. Bernard’s 2005 The King’s Reformation sees the executions as evidence that Henry himself drove the radical edge of religious change — not Cromwell. Diarmaid MacCulloch credits Cromwell with the legal architecture and the 1536 evangelical injunctions, but agrees the king set the appetite for capital punishment of dissent. John Guy stresses how rare and shocking the execution of a senior bishop and a former Lord Chancellor was in early modern Europe; the deaths of Fisher and More became propaganda gifts to Catholic powers and shaped the future of English Catholic identity.

before.content_html:
In 1535 there were roughly 800 religious houses in England and Wales, holding around a fifth of the country’s landed wealth and employing some 10,000 monks, nuns and friars. By 1540 every single one of them had been suppressed, their land sold, their plate melted down and their buildings stripped or pulled down for stone. It was the largest transfer of property in English history before the modern era. The official justification was the reform of corrupt religion. The real outcome — though framed in spiritual language — was a fiscal and political revolution that bound the gentry of England to the new Tudor regime.

Religious Houses in Local Communities

Before 1535 monasteries were embedded in every region of England. They were landlords renting farms to tenants, employers of servants and labourers, hosts of travellers, schools for the local gentry’s sons, and almoners distributing food to the poor at the gate. Larger houses such as Glastonbury, Fountains and Reading had incomes greater than most peers of the realm. Smaller ones were tiny — sometimes only three or four monks — and often poorly run. Either way they were the most visible institutions of medieval Christianity in their local communities, and a Mass said in their churches was understood to relieve souls in purgatory.

The crown’s attack therefore did not begin in a vacuum. Reformers including Erasmus had long mocked monastic laxity, and Wolsey had already dissolved 29 smaller houses in the 1520s to fund his colleges at Oxford and Ipswich. Cromwell himself had cut his administrative teeth on Wolsey’s closures. What was new in 1535 was the scale, the speed, and the legal machinery that turned a long-running reformist trend into a complete suppression.

Key Fact

Around 800 religious houses operated in England and Wales in 1535, holding roughly a fifth of the country’s landed wealth. They acted as landlords, employers, almsgivers, hostels for travellers and schools for the gentry — their suppression touched every county.

Cromwell’s Commissions of 1535

As Vicegerent in Spirituals, Cromwell launched two parallel surveys in 1535. The first was the Valor Ecclesiasticus, a county-by-county valuation of every benefice and religious house in the country. Conducted by gentry commissioners and finished in months, it produced the most accurate picture of monastic wealth ever compiled. The total annual income was put at around £165,000 — a sum that dwarfed the king’s ordinary revenue.

The second survey, conducted by visitors including Richard Layton and Thomas Legh, was a moral inspection. They asked questions designed to elicit damaging answers: about sexual conduct, about superstitious relics, about disobedience to royal authority. Their reports — the Comperta — landed on Cromwell’s desk by early 1536 and were a catalogue of (selectively) shocking abuses. Whether the abuses were widespread is debatable. The reports’ political function was not in doubt: they provided the justification for legislation already drafted.

The 1536 Act: Smaller Houses First

The Act for the Suppression of the Lesser Monasteries of March 1536 dissolved every house with an annual income under £200, citing the ‘manifest sin, vicious, carnal and abominable living’ uncovered by the visitors. It targeted around 300 smaller houses and was carefully framed as a reforming measure: larger, ‘great and solemn’ monasteries were left standing, and their abbots reassured. The 1536 Act was the thin end of the wedge. Land and rents from the dissolved houses passed to a new department, the Court of Augmentations, set up specifically to manage them and to channel the income to the crown.

The Comperta reports were genuine, but they were also one-sided and politically commissioned. The National Archives’ research summary on the dissolutions makes the point clearly: fiscal motives mattered as much as religious ones. Royal income from monastic land roughly doubled crown revenue in the late 1530s, and most of that wealth was sold off in the 1540s to fund Henry’s wars in France and Scotland. Diarmaid MacCulloch argues Cromwell genuinely wanted reform — an English Bible, a literate parish clergy — but agrees that without the financial prize, Henry would never have signed off on a complete suppression.

The 1539 Act: The Greater Houses Fall

After the Pilgrimage of Grace was crushed in 1537 and several leading abbots were implicated, the larger houses lost their political protection. Through 1538 and 1539 commissioners moved through them one by one, using a combination of legal pressure, threats of treason charges, and the offer of generous pensions for compliant abbots. Most surrendered ‘voluntarily’. The Second Act of Dissolution of 1539 simply legalised what was happening on the ground. The last great abbey, Waltham, was surrendered in March 1540. The four-and-a-half-century-old institution of English monasticism was extinguished in less than five years.

Beneficiaries and Losers

The crown was the immediate beneficiary. Annual royal revenue rose by something like £130,000, doubling the king’s ordinary income. But Henry did not keep the land. By the end of the 1540s, around two thirds of monastic estates had been sold or granted away — mostly to the gentry, lawyers and merchant families who could afford the prices. This was a deliberate policy choice. By selling, the crown raised cash for war and bound a wide layer of property-owners to the Reformation: anyone who bought monastic land would lose it if the old religion ever came back.

The losers were equally clear. Around 10,000 monks, nuns and friars were displaced; senior figures received pensions, but lay servants and the urban poor who had relied on monastic alms generally received nothing. commissioners stripped lead from roofs, pulled down towers and sold building stone for re-use. Local economies built around monastic markets and pilgrimage routes lost their anchor. In the north of England, where monastic landholding was particularly heavy and the parish clergy thin, the suppression was understood as the destruction of a way of life — and helped fuel the rebellion that broke out in autumn 1536.

Key Fact

Crown income roughly doubled to around £295,000 a year by the late 1530s, but two thirds of monastic land was sold off in the 1540s. The buyers were the gentry, lawyers and merchants — the social group most invested in the new regime. The biggest losers were the displaced monastic servants and the urban poor.

G.W. Bernard’s The King’s Reformation (2005) emphasises Henry’s personal appetite for monastic wealth and his suspicion of any institution outside royal control. Diarmaid MacCulloch’s Thomas Cromwell: A Revolutionary Life (2018) argues Cromwell’s evangelical convictions made him a genuine reformer who saw monasticism as bad theology, not just rich theology — though he was happy to take the cash. The National Archives’ research guide stresses the long fiscal afterlife: the sales of the 1540s created a new gentry landowning class with a permanent stake in the Reformation. All three perspectives can be true at once.

practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the financial motive against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Arguments for ‘most important’:
• The Valor Ecclesiasticus of 1535 produced a precise fiscal target before any moral case had been built — the survey’s purpose was financial.
• The Court of Augmentations was created specifically to channel monastic income to the crown.
• Royal revenue roughly doubled, allowing Henry to fund the wars of the 1540s without ruinous taxation.
• Two thirds of monastic land was sold within a decade — the crown took the cash rather than holding the estates for ongoing reform.
• The smaller houses were dissolved first because they were the easier and less politically costly target, not because they were the most theologically problematic.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• Religious conviction — Cromwell’s evangelicalism, Cranmer’s 1536 Ten Articles and the new royal injunctions show genuine Reformation purpose.
• The Comperta reports — whatever their reliability, they reflected real reformist concerns about monastic standards stretching back to Erasmus and Wolsey’s 1520s closures.
• Royal supremacy — monasteries owed their authority to the Pope; their existence was incompatible with the 1534 Act of Supremacy.
• Political binding — the deliberate sales of monastic land to gentry buyers created a propertied class invested in the Reformation surviving.
• Henry’s personality — G.W. Bernard argues Henry himself drove the appetite for the suppressions, not just Cromwell.

Overall judgement: financial considerations made the suppression worth doing on this scale; religious and political considerations made it possible to justify and to consolidate. A top-band answer weighs these motives explicitly and explains how they reinforced each other.
