before.content_html:
In October 1536, six months after the first monasteries had been suppressed, Lincolnshire and Yorkshire rose against the regime in what became the largest popular rebellion of Tudor England. At its height, around 30,000 men marched under the banner of the Five Wounds of Christ — more than the standing royal army. They called their movement a pilgrimage, not a rebellion. Within four months it was over. Robert Aske, who had reframed sedition as religious devotion, was hanging in chains at York. Cromwell’s programme survived its sternest test — but only because the Duke of Norfolk had been willing to lie.

Why the North Rose: A Tangle of Grievances

Religion was the most visible cause but not the only one. The dissolution of the smaller monasteries earlier in 1536 hit the north hardest, where monastic landholding was concentrated and the parish clergy thin. Local communities saw familiar abbeys threatened, gate-alms cut off, and unfamiliar ‘commissioners’ arriving to take inventories. Rumours spread that parish church plate, baptismal fonts and even weddings would soon be taxed.

Religion sat alongside fiscal grievances. The 1534 Subsidy Act extended taxation in peacetime — previously taxation had been linked to war — and the 1535 collection bit hardest in a year of poor harvests. The Statute of Uses (1536) threatened the gentry’s long-standing tax-avoidance arrangements over land. Agrarian grievances over enclosures and high rents added a third layer. Northern political grievances completed the mix: lords like Lord Darcy and the Percy family resented the rise of low-born advisers like Cromwell, the loss of regional autonomy and the new Council of the North.

Key Fact

The Pilgrimage of Grace combined religious grievances over the dissolution of the monasteries, fiscal anger at the 1534 Subsidy and 1536 Statute of Uses, agrarian protest against rents and enclosures, and northern political resentment of Cromwell and the loss of regional autonomy. Lincolnshire rose first in October 1536.

Lincolnshire Rises, October 1536

The trouble began at Louth in Lincolnshire on 1 October 1536. Royal commissioners arriving to inspect a church were chased from the town. By 4 October, several thousand commoners and parish priests had gathered at Caistor and Horncastle, then marched on Lincoln. They issued the Lincoln Articles, attacking the dissolution, the Statute of Uses, the Subsidy and the ‘low-born’ ministers around the king. Henry replied with a contemptuous proclamation calling the rebels ‘rude commons of one of the most brute and beastly shires in the whole realm’. Lincolnshire’s gentry leaders quickly lost their nerve and dispersed the host by 14 October.

Robert Aske’s Pilgrimage, October–December 1536

As the Lincolnshire rising collapsed, a far larger movement broke out across Yorkshire. Its leader was Robert Aske, a Yorkshire lawyer who had been in London during the Lincolnshire trouble. Aske was a brilliant organiser. He gave the rising a new name — the Pilgrimage of Grace — reframing rebellion as religious devotion. He composed an oath of loyalty to king, commonwealth and church that allowed gentry and commoners to march together. By 16 October, York surrendered to him without a shot. By 21 October, Pontefract Castle — held by the elderly Lord Darcy — surrendered too. Hull fell next.

By the end of October, Aske commanded around 30,000 men — the largest force in England. From Pontefract he issued the more developed Pontefract Articles. Their demands were sweeping: restore the dissolved monasteries, repeal the Statute of Uses, dismiss Cromwell and Cranmer, condemn heresy, hold a free Parliament in the north, and recognise Princess Mary as legitimate. The articles showed how religion, fiscal grievance, faction politics and dynastic concern braided together.

Religion was the rallying banner, but the historians M.E. James and C.S.L. Davies have shown the rising drew on overlapping fiscal, agrarian and political grievances. The 1535 subsidy bit hard, harvests had failed in 1535, the Statute of Uses threatened the gentry’s land arrangements, and northern lords resented losing regional autonomy. Robert Aske re-framed sedition as ‘pilgrimage’ precisely because the motives were so mixed: a religious banner could unite groups whose individual grievances were not the same. Treating the rising as purely religious misses why it could mobilise 30,000 men so quickly.

Norfolk’s Negotiations at Doncaster

The Duke of Norfolk, sent north with a small royal force of around 8,000 men, knew he could not win a battle. On 27 October at Doncaster, he opened negotiations with the rebels under a flag of truce. He played for time, promising a pardon and a free Parliament in York to discuss the rebels’ grievances. Privately, both Norfolk and Henry knew the promises were tactical. Aske, a lawyer who took oaths seriously, persuaded the rebel host to disperse and travelled to London to meet Henry in person at Christmas 1536. He was reassured, given a velvet jacket, and sent home.

Bigod’s Rising and the Reckoning, 1537

The truce held only weeks. In January 1537, when promised concessions failed to appear, Sir Francis Bigod launched a smaller, badly organised rising in the East Riding. Aske and Lord Darcy publicly denounced it, but the rising gave Henry the legal cover he had been waiting for. The first pardon, he ruled, had been broken — by association if not by act. Norfolk returned north under martial law in February 1537 with orders to make examples. Around 216 people were executed, including Robert Aske, hanged in chains at Clifford’s Tower in York in July 1537. Lord Darcy was beheaded on Tower Hill, Sir Robert Constable hanged at Hull. Bodies were left in chains as warnings.

Key Fact

Norfolk negotiated a pardon at Doncaster in October 1536 to disperse the rebel host of around 30,000. After Bigod’s January 1537 rising broke the truce, Norfolk returned under martial law and oversaw around 216 executions, including Robert Aske, hanged in chains at York in July 1537.

Aftermath and Significance

In the short term, the regime survived. The dissolution of the larger monasteries went ahead in 1538–40, the Council of the North was reformed under royal control, and the gentry of the north absorbed monastic land like their southern counterparts. In the long term, the Pilgrimage taught Tudor governments that the north could not be governed casually. Henry never again travelled there in person. Cromwell’s reputation among the conservatives never recovered — the Duke of Norfolk and Bishop Gardiner now had a permanent grievance to rehearse.

M.E. James emphasised the role of social hierarchy — commoners, gentry and northern lords each had distinct reasons to march, but the ‘pilgrimage’ banner allowed a temporary alliance. C.S.L. Davies stressed the fiscal trigger: the 1535 subsidy collected during a bad harvest year was the immediate match. R.W. Hoyle’s 2001 study foregrounded Robert Aske as a serious political thinker whose ‘pilgrimage’ framing was a calculated political move, not naive piety. All three readings argue against a purely religious interpretation, while accepting that religion was the language in which the grievances were expressed.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Pilgrimage of Grace combined four causes — the dissolution of the monasteries, the 1534 Subsidy and 1536 Statute of Uses, agrarian grievance over rents and enclosures, and northern political resentment of Cromwell and the new Council of the North.
  • Lincolnshire rose first on 1 October 1536 and dispersed within two weeks. The main rising was the Yorkshire Pilgrimage led by the lawyer Robert Aske, which mustered around 30,000 men, took York and Pontefract, and issued the 24 Pontefract Articles in December 1536.
  • The Duke of Norfolk negotiated a tactical pardon at Doncaster, then used Bigod’s January 1537 rising as cover to declare martial law. Around 216 people were executed, including Aske, hanged in chains at York in July 1537. The dissolution programme continued unchecked.

For 16-mark judgements, the discriminating point at the top band is whether you can weigh these factors against each other and explain how the ‘pilgrimage’ banner united motives that would otherwise have been incompatible. Use precise period vocabulary — ‘commissioners’, ‘subsidy’, ‘attainder’, ‘martial law’, ‘Pontefract Articles’.

before.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark judgement question on Cromwell’s fall, weigh three factors explicitly: the Cleves marriage as the immediate trigger, the conservative faction (Norfolk, Catherine Howard, Gardiner) as the political weapon, and the wider problem that Cromwell’s evangelical religious agenda had outrun what Henry actually wanted. Use the language of the period — ‘attainder’, ‘Privy Council’, ‘Vicegerent’, ‘annulment’, not ‘divorce’. The SPaG mark on these questions rewards consistent technical Tudor vocabulary. The strongest answers also note the structural irony: Cromwell was condemned by the same Act of Attainder he had perfected against his own enemies.
before.content_html:
Between 1534 and 1540 Thomas Cromwell rebuilt the machinery of English government, managed the king through three new marriages, and orchestrated the fall of the most famous queen in Tudor history. Then, in the space of three months in the summer of 1540, the same machinery turned on him. He went to the block on Tower Hill on 28 July with a German bride still officially Henry’s wife and a conservative faction in command of the Privy Chamber. The story of Cromwell’s last six years is the story of Tudor government modernising under one minister — and then proving, decisively, that the king was still in charge.

The Fall of Anne Boleyn, May 1536

Anne Boleyn had been Cromwell’s political ally during the break with Rome. By spring 1536, that alliance had broken. The two clashed over how monastic wealth should be spent — Anne wanted it directed to education and charity, Cromwell wanted it to fund the crown and to bind gentry buyers to the Reformation. They also disagreed over foreign policy: Anne favoured France, Cromwell wanted reconciliation with Charles V’s empire after Catherine of Aragon’s death in January 1536. Anne had also failed to produce a male heir; her January 1536 miscarriage of a son weighed heavily on Henry.

In late April 1536 Cromwell took action. Five men were arrested on charges of adultery with the queen, including her brother George (incest) and the court musician Mark Smeaton, the only one who confessed — almost certainly under torture. Henry Norris denied everything to the end. Anne was arrested on 2 May, tried at the Tower on 15 May, and convicted by a jury that included her own uncle, the Duke of Norfolk, and her former suitor Henry Percy. Cranmer annulled the marriage on 17 May; Anne was beheaded with a French sword on 19 May 1536. Within ten days Henry had married Jane Seymour.

Key Fact

Anne Boleyn fell because she clashed with Cromwell over the use of monastic wealth and over the imperial alliance, and because she had failed to produce a male heir. She was arrested on 2 May 1536, convicted on charges of adultery and incest, and beheaded on 19 May. Henry married Jane Seymour ten days later.

Jane Seymour and the Birth of Edward, 1537

Jane Seymour was a quiet conservative member of the Privy Chamber who had served both of Henry’s previous wives. Her appeal lay in her gentleness and her conservative religious sympathies, which steadied an exhausted king. She used her influence carefully: most famously interceding to ask for the restoration of the dissolved abbeys at the height of the Pilgrimage of Grace — Henry told her sharply not to meddle in his affairs. On 12 October 1537, after a long labour, she gave birth to a son: Prince Edward, Henry’s long-awaited male heir. Twelve days later, on 24 October, Jane died of puerperal fever. Henry mourned her for years.

Reform of Government and Royal Finance

In the same years Cromwell continued to remake government. Geoffrey Elton called this a ‘Tudor revolution in government’; later historians (John Guy, David Starkey) think the changes were piecemeal. Either way the changes were real. Cromwell turned the office of Principal Secretary into the central coordinating role of Tudor government. He created new revenue departments — the Court of Augmentations to manage monastic income, the Court of First Fruits and Tenths to manage church revenues, the Court of Wards for feudal incomes, and the Court of General Surveyors. Each had a permanent staff and account books separate from the medieval Exchequer.

Cromwell also began the transition from the medieval royal household to a smaller, more formal Privy Council. By 1540 around 19 named councillors met regularly with formal agendas and clerks taking minutes — the predecessor of the modern Cabinet. Whether all of this counts as a ‘revolution’ is debated, but contemporaries certainly noticed: government in 1540 was conducted in writing, through department heads, with parliamentary statute as the engine of policy — very different from the personal monarchy of 1509.

Geoffrey Elton’s 1953 book The Tudor Revolution in Government argued Cromwell deliberately built a modern, bureaucratic state — Privy Council, secretary of state, parliamentary statute as the engine of policy. Revisionists led by John Guy and David Starkey have argued the changes were responses to immediate problems rather than a planned revolution. Diarmaid MacCulloch’s 2018 biography agrees Cromwell was a brilliant administrator but locates his deepest motive in evangelical religious conviction. The revisionist position is now mainstream, but every reading agrees Cromwell concentrated more government in fewer hands than any English minister had previously managed.

Management of Parliament

Cromwell’s most lasting innovation was his use of parliamentary statute as the engine of state. Between 1532 and 1540 the Reformation Parliament passed legislation of a scope no medieval monarch could have imagined: the Acts in Restraint of Appeals (1533), of Supremacy (1534), of Succession (1534), the two Acts of Dissolution, the Statute of Uses (1536), and the Act of Six Articles (1539). Cromwell drafted bills, lobbied MPs through patronage and persuasion, and managed proceedings on the floor of the Commons. He treated Parliament as a working partner in government, not merely a tax-granting body. The medieval doctrine that the king-in-Parliament was the highest authority in the realm was now operating practice.

The Cleves Marriage Disaster, 1539–40

By 1539, Catholic Europe was reuniting under Pope Paul III’s diplomatic offensive. Charles V and Francis I had signed the Truce of Nice (1538), and Cromwell feared a joint Catholic invasion. His response was a Protestant alliance: a marriage between Henry and Anne of Cleves, sister of the Protestant Duke of Cleves on the Lower Rhine. Hans Holbein the Younger was sent to paint her in 1539. Cromwell’s ambassadors enthused over her appearance. Henry, looking at the portrait, agreed.

When Anne arrived at Rochester on New Year’s Eve 1539, Henry made his trademark surprise visit in disguise to greet his future wife. He found her plain-looking, awkward in the language and unsuited to courtly flirtation. The marriage went ahead on 6 January 1540 because cancelling would humiliate the German alliance, but Henry was furious. He told Cromwell that he ‘liked her not’. Within weeks the king was seeking grounds for an annulment. Anne, sensibly, agreed to it; the marriage was declared void on 9 July 1540, and she was rewarded with manors and the title of ‘the king’s sister’.

Key Fact

Cromwell arranged the marriage to Anne of Cleves in late 1539 to build a Protestant alliance against a feared Catholic coalition between Charles V and Francis I. Henry found Anne unattractive in person on New Year’s Eve 1539 but went through with the wedding on 6 January 1540. The marriage was annulled on 9 July 1540, three weeks before Cromwell’s execution.

The Fall, June–July 1540

Cromwell’s enemies moved fast. The Duke of Norfolk, his niece Catherine Howard, and Bishop Stephen Gardiner formed the conservative faction. Through spring 1540 they presented Catherine, a teenage cousin of Anne Boleyn, to the king at Norfolk’s house in Lambeth. Henry was infatuated. By June, with the Cleves marriage looking like a personal humiliation, Henry was prepared to listen to the conservatives’ long-running case against Cromwell — that he was a heretic who had pushed evangelical reform too far, and a low-born minister now elevated above his station as Earl of Essex (April 1540).

On 10 June 1540, at a Privy Council meeting, Norfolk personally tore the Order of the Garter from Cromwell’s neck and accused him of treason and heresy. Cromwell was arrested without trial, denied a hearing, and condemned by Act of Attainder — the same legal weapon he had used against the Nun of Kent and Anne Boleyn. Henry kept him alive long enough to provide a witness statement on the Cleves annulment, then executed him on Tower Hill on 28 July 1540 — the same day Henry married Catherine Howard. The man who had concentrated more power than any commoner in English history died on charges he was given no chance to answer.

Diarmaid MacCulloch’s 2018 biography argues the Cleves marriage was the trigger but not the cause: Cromwell had accumulated too many enemies and pushed evangelical reform faster than Henry comfortably wanted. G.W. Bernard’s The King’s Reformation stresses Henry’s personal anger at being humiliated and his susceptibility to conservative arguments once Catherine Howard had caught his eye. Geoffrey Elton saw the fall as a contingent disaster — a gifted minister destroyed by court faction politics. The shared judgement is that Cromwell’s methods (attainder, oaths, surveillance) had created precisely the legal arsenal his enemies could now turn on him.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Cromwell’s reform of royal finance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature: 1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail.

Indicative content:
• Court of Augmentations — the new department created to channel monastic income from the dissolution to the crown.
• Court of First Fruits and Tenths — managed church revenues such as the first year’s income from a benefice paid to the crown.
• Court of Wards — administered feudal incomes from the heirs of tenants-in-chief.
• Court of General Surveyors — supervised crown lands and existing royal estates.
• Specialist staff — each department had permanent officers and account books separate from the medieval Exchequer.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Two features but detail vague.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the marriage to Anne of Cleves.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for each feature.

Indicative content:
• Diplomatic purpose — the match was arranged by Cromwell in 1539 to build a Protestant alliance after Charles V and Francis I had signed the Truce of Nice.
• Anne’s background — she was the sister of the Duke of Cleves, a Protestant prince on the Lower Rhine.
• The Holbein portrait — the king relied on Hans Holbein the Younger’s 1539 painting and ambassadorial reports before agreeing to the match.
• The Rochester meeting — Henry made a surprise visit in disguise on New Year’s Eve 1539 and found Anne plain-looking and awkward.
• The annulment — the marriage was declared void on 9 July 1540 with Anne’s cooperation; she was rewarded with manors and the title ‘the king’s sister’.

Mastering: Two precise features with accurate detail.
Secure: Two features with relevant detail.
Developing: Detail vague or partly inaccurate.
Emerging: One feature only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Anne Boleyn fell from power in 1536.
You may use the following in your answer:
• Thomas Cromwell
• the failure to produce a male heir
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Clash with Cromwell — Anne and Cromwell disagreed over how monastic wealth should be spent (charity vs crown finance).
• Foreign policy disagreement — after Catherine of Aragon’s death in January 1536, Cromwell wanted reconciliation with Charles V; Anne preferred the French alliance.
• Failure to produce a male heir — Anne’s January 1536 miscarriage of a son weighed heavily on Henry, who needed a Tudor male heir.
• Henry’s infatuation with Jane Seymour — the king’s eye had moved on by spring 1536.
• Charges of adultery and incest — Cromwell engineered the case using forced confessions (Mark Smeaton) and the testimony of court enemies.
• Family abandonment — even her uncle, the Duke of Norfolk, sat on the jury that convicted her, showing the Boleyn faction had collapsed.

Mastering: Three or more explained reasons with both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Description without focus on causation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cromwell’s reforms of government had a lasting impact on Tudor England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Privy Council
• parliamentary statute
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained, supported reasons.

Indicative content:
• Privy Council — the smaller, formal council with named councillors and minutes replaced the larger medieval royal household and shaped Tudor government for the rest of the century.
• Parliamentary statute — turning Acts of Parliament into the engine of policy created a constitutional precedent that outlived Cromwell himself.
• Specialised revenue courts — Augmentations, First Fruits, Wards and General Surveyors gave the crown professional financial machinery.
• Principal Secretary — Cromwell’s use of the office created a model for later secretaries of state under Cecil and Walsingham.
• Use of commissioners — reliance on gentry commissioners for nationwide tasks (Valor Ecclesiasticus, suppression) became the standard Tudor method of local administration.
• Bureaucratic record-keeping — Cromwell’s correspondence and accounts established the habit of governing in writing rather than by personal proclamation.

Mastering: Three or more reasons explained with precise detail; both stimulus points developed.
Secure: Two or three reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation thin.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Cromwell fell from power in 1540.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the marriage to Anne of Cleves
• the Duke of Norfolk
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for sustained explanation of multiple reasons.

Indicative content:
• Cleves marriage failure — Henry found Anne plain-looking and awkward; the marriage humiliated him personally and discredited Cromwell’s diplomatic judgement.
• Conservative faction — the Duke of Norfolk, Bishop Stephen Gardiner and Catherine Howard’s family worked together against Cromwell.
• Catherine Howard — presented to Henry at Norfolk’s Lambeth house, the teenage Howard cousin gave the king a personal motive to be free of Cleves and Cromwell.
• Henry’s religious conservatism — the Act of Six Articles (1539) had already shown Henry was uncomfortable with Cromwell’s evangelical pace.
• Cromwell’s low-born status — his April 1540 promotion to Earl of Essex provoked further conservative anger that a commoner sat above old peers.
• Use of attainder — Cromwell was condemned without trial, by the same Act of Attainder weapon he had used against the Nun of Kent and Anne Boleyn.
• The diplomatic context — the feared Charles V–Francis I coalition turned out to be less imminent than Cromwell had argued, weakening the case for Cleves.
• Henry’s personal authority — the king demonstrated by Cromwell’s fall that even his most powerful minister served at royal pleasure.

Mastering: Five or more reasons explained with precise evidence; both stimulus points developed; clear argument throughout.
Secure: Three or four reasons with relevant explanation.
Developing: Reasons identified but explanation patchy.
Emerging: Largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
‘The main reason for Cromwell’s fall in 1540 was the failure of the marriage to Anne of Cleves.’
How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Duke of Norfolk
• Cromwell’s religious convictions
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Reward sustained argument that weighs the Cleves marriage against alternative causes and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. SPaG awarded for consistent accurate use of period-specific terminology.

Arguments for ‘most important’:
• The Cleves marriage humiliated Henry personally on New Year’s Eve 1539 and tied Cromwell to that humiliation.
• Cromwell’s ambassadors had reported favourably on Anne; the failure was a direct intelligence failure on his part.
• The marriage produced no heir and damaged Cromwell’s standing in just six months.
• The annulment process kept Cromwell alive only as a witness for the king’s case.
• The diplomatic justification weakened: the feared Charles V–Francis I coalition had stalled.

Arguments for alternative explanations:
• The Duke of Norfolk and Bishop Gardiner had been working against Cromwell for years and only needed an opportunity.
• Catherine Howard — the king’s infatuation gave the conservative faction a Howard candidate to put forward.
• Religious conviction — Cromwell had pushed evangelical reform faster than Henry wanted; the 1539 Act of Six Articles was already a corrective signal.
• Faction politics — the conservative court had blamed Cromwell for monastic suppression and the Pilgrimage of Grace casualties.
• Cromwell’s low-born status — his elevation to Earl of Essex in April 1540 antagonised noble rivals.
• Use of his own methods — the Act of Attainder he was condemned by was a weapon he had perfected.
• Henry’s personality — Diarmaid MacCulloch and G.W. Bernard agree the king himself decided to drop Cromwell once the political price became higher than the value.

Overall judgement: the Cleves marriage was the trigger that turned a long-running political vulnerability into a fatal crisis. Cromwell’s religious agenda, his low-born status, and the conservative faction’s patience all mattered more for explaining why he was vulnerable in the first place. A top-band answer weighs these factors and reaches a substantiated conclusion using precise Tudor vocabulary.

Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument; multiple factors weighed; substantiated overall judgement; precise period vocabulary throughout; consistent SPaG accuracy.
Secure: Argument addresses both sides; conclusion reached; mostly accurate SPaG.
Developing: Some argument with relevant evidence but limited weighing; SPaG inconsistent.
Emerging: Largely descriptive; SPaG limited.
